children.title: Potentially Optimal Rectangle Principle
children.top_down_role: Equivalent selection representations linking region size, sampled value, and implicit regularity scales.

assumptions_latex: The active rectangles form a finite family \(\{R_i\}_{i=1}^m\).
Each \(R_i\) is represented by a size \(d_i\ge 0\) and sampled center value \(f_i\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rectangles minimizing \(f_i-Kd_i\) for some \(K>0\) correspond to size-value points on a lower supporting face of the finite point set, before any sufficient-improvement filter is applied.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-dimensional geometric encoding of DIRECT's scale-dependent comparison.

source_refs.locator: Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case, p. 39

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Map each active rectangle \(R_i\) to \(p_i=(d_i,f_i)\). For fixed \(K>0\), minimizing \(f_i-Kd_i\) is equivalent to translating a line of slope \(K\) upward until it first meets the finite size-value set. Thus every minimizing point lies on a lower supporting face with positive slope; points in the relative interior of a supported edge may qualify and need not be exposed points. Among points with equal size, only those having the smallest center value can qualify.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Plotting size against center value turns the scale comparison into a supporting-line problem; eligible points lie on a positive-slope lower supporting face, including points along a supported edge.
knowledge_statements.title: Rectangle Size–Value Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case, p. 39

assumptions_latex: The active size-value set \(P=\{(d_i,f_i)\}_{i=1}^m\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rectangles minimizing \(f_i-Kd_i\) for some \(K>0\) are exactly the lower-hull points admitting a supporting line of positive slope.

notation.meaning: Finite set of active size-value points
Lower convex hull of the active point set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-line characterization before the sufficient-improvement filter is imposed.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Convex Hull p. 12
Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case p. 39

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{(d_i,f_i):1\le i\le m\}\), an index \(i\) minimizes \(f_j-Kd_j\) over all \(j\) for some \(K>0\) if and only if a line \(y=Kx+b\) supports \(P\) from below at \((d_i,f_i)\). Consequently, all such points belong to the lower convex hull \(H_-(P)\), including every point on a supported hull edge. Equal-size points above the lowest value and points strictly above the lower hull are never selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rectangle passes the scale-dependent comparison exactly when its size-value point admits a positive-slope supporting line on the lower convex hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Convex-Hull Selection

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Convex Hull p. 12
Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case p. 39

assumptions_latex: The active rectangles form a finite family \(\{R_i\}_{i=1}^m\).
Each \(R_i\) has center value \(f_i\in\mathbb{R}\) and size \(d_i\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every rectangle minimizing \(f_i-Kd_i\) for some \(K>0\) is Pareto efficient for minimizing \(f_i\) and maximizing \(d_i\), but the converse can fail.

notation.meaning: Center value and size of rectangle i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relationship between bicriteria nondominance and supported DIRECT selection.

source_refs.locator: Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case, p. 39

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Say that \(R_j\) dominates \(R_i\) when \(f_j\le f_i\) and \(d_j\ge d_i\), with at least one strict inequality. If \(R_i\) minimizes \(f_\ell-Kd_\ell\) over \(1\le\ell\le m\) for some \(K>0\), then no rectangle dominates it, because domination would imply \(f_j-Kd_j<f_i-Kd_i\). Hence every scale-supported choice is Pareto efficient for minimizing \(f_i\) and maximizing \(d_i\). The converse can fail because a nondominated point strictly above the lower convex hull minimizes no score of this form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale-supported DIRECT rectangles are nondominated with respect to low value and large size, but unsupported Pareto points above the lower hull need not be selected.
knowledge_statements.title: Pareto-Lipschitzian Selection

source_witnesses.locator: Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case, p. 39

assumptions_latex: The active rectangles form a finite family \(\{R_i\}_{i=1}^m\), with center values \(f_i\in\mathbb{R}\) and sizes \(d_i\ge 0\).
The incumbent is \(f_{\min}=\min_{1\le j\le m}f_j\), and \(\varepsilon\ge 0\) is prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scale-dependent comparison admits both value-favored and size-favored rectangles, while the sufficient-improvement inequality removes candidates whose predicted lower score is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical DIRECT eligibility with a relative sufficient-improvement filter.

source_refs.locator: Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case, p. 39

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An active rectangle \(R_i\) is eligible when there exists \(K>0\) such that \(f_i-Kd_i\le f_j-Kd_j\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(f_i-Kd_i\le f_{\min}-\varepsilon|f_{\min}|\). Small \(K\) gives greater relative influence to low sampled values, whereas large \(K\) gives greater relative influence to large sizes. The second inequality removes supported candidates whose predicted lower score does not improve sufficiently on the incumbent under this scaling convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DIRECT scans positive scales to admit both low-value and large-size candidates, then applies a relative predicted-improvement condition controlled by epsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Global–Local Selection Bias Control

source_witnesses.locator: Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case, p. 39

children.title: DIRECT Partition-Sampling Variants
children.top_down_role: Variants distinguished by cell geometry, representative points, and subdivision operators.

assumptions_latex: A selected rectangle has at least one longest coordinate.
The variant processes exactly one longest coordinate per partition operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each operation produces three children by trisecting one chosen longest side and requires at most two new objective evaluations.

notation.meaning: One third of the chosen full side length

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-coordinate trisection variant; the exact published tie and selection rules remain source-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a selected rectangle centered at \(c\) with half-lengths \(h_j\), choose one index \(j^*\inoperatorname*{argmax}_j h_j\) by the variant's tie rule and set \(delta=2h_{j^*}/3\). Evaluate \(f(c-delta e_{j^*})\) and \(f(c+delta e_{j^*})\) unless already known, then cut perpendicular to coordinate \(j^*\) at \(c_{j^*}pmdelta/2\). Replace the parent by the resulting three equal-width children, retain the corresponding centers and values, recompute their sizes, and return them to the active rectangle set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This DIRECT variant trisects only one chosen longest side per selected rectangle, creating three children with at most two new center evaluations.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Long-Side DIRECT

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct role, but this named DIRECT variant has no citation, and its tie rule and inherited selection rule are explicitly unresolved. The statement also contains multiple malformed commands (`inoperatorname`, `delta`, and `pm`). Because the exact published variant cannot be determined reliably without a source, a replacement should not be inferred from the generic trisection description.

assumptions_latex: The objective is a deterministic function \(f:[0,1]^n\to\mathbb{R}\).
The current partition consists of axis-aligned rectangles with stored diagonal sample values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the best sampled point and its objective value after the prescribed evaluation or partition budget.

notation.meaning: opposite diagonal sample points of rectangle R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Family-level BIRECT template; exact variants may use different diagonal points and longest-side bisections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\mathcal{R}_0=\{[0,1]^n\}\) and evaluate \(f\) at two prescribed points \(u_R,v_R\) on a main diagonal. At iteration \(k\), assign every \(R\in\mathcal{R}_k\) a representative value \(m_R=\min\{f(u_R),f(v_R)\}\) and size \(d_R\). Select rectangles that are nondominated for the family criterion based on \((d_R,m_R)\). For each selected rectangle, bisect a longest side, retain reusable diagonal values, and evaluate the missing diagonal points of its children. Continue until the evaluation or partition budget is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: BIRECT repeatedly selects promising rectangles using size and diagonal samples, bisects a longest side, reuses inherited values, and returns the best sampled point.
knowledge_statements.title: BIRECT Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits this method-family container, but no evidence is supplied for the defining diagonal samples, size-value criterion, bisection convention, or value-reuse rule. Those details distinguish BIRECT variants and cannot be verified from the record alone.

assumptions_latex: The objective is a deterministic function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) on a compact hyperrectangle \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\).
Every active rectangle has objective values at prescribed points on one or more diagonals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method returns the sampled point having the smallest observed objective value.

notation.meaning: active rectangle partition at iteration k
diagonal sample set of rectangle R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic DIRECT-type diagonal-sampling scheme, not a specification of one named implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\mathcal{R}_0=\{D\}\) and evaluate \(f\) on the prescribed diagonal sample set \(S_D\). At iteration \(k\), compute for each \(R\in\mathcal{R}_k\) a characteristic \(q_R\) from its diameter and the values \(\{f(x):x\in S_R\}\). Select rectangles that are potentially optimal under the method's size-value rule. Partition each selected rectangle along designated longest coordinates, form each child's diagonal sample set, and evaluate only points whose values cannot be inherited. Stop at the prescribed budget or tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: These methods rank rectangles using objective values sampled on diagonals, subdivide potentially optimal rectangles, and reuse shared endpoint values when possible.
knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal-Sampling DIRECT-Type Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the container, but the characteristic q_R, diagonal sample construction, potentially-optimal rule, and subdivision convention are method-defining and left generic without a source.

assumptions_latex: The objective is a deterministic function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) on a compact polytope \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\).
A finite simplicial partition of \(D\) and a fixed simplex subdivision rule are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the best objective value and sampled point generated before termination.

notation.meaning: representative sample point of simplex T

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplicial analogue of DIRECT with a generic potentially-optimal size-value selection rule.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Partition Methods on General Convex and Star Sets p. 119

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a finite simplicial partition \(\mathcal{T}_0\) of \(D\) and evaluate \(f(c_T)\) for every initial simplex \(T\). At iteration \(k\), associate each \(T\in\mathcal{T}_k\) with \((d_T,f(c_T))\), select simplices that are potentially optimal for some positive unknown regularity constant, and subdivide each selected simplex by the fixed conforming rule. Evaluate the representative points of new simplices, reusing coincident samples. Stop when the evaluation budget, minimum diameter, or target accuracy condition is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplicial DIRECT-type method selects simplices by size and sampled value, subdivides the selected simplices, and records the best sampled point.
knowledge_statements.title: Simplicial DIRECT-Type Methods

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Partition Methods on General Convex and Star Sets p. 119

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited general section on partition methods does not specifically substantiate the stated simplicial DIRECT algorithm, including representative points, selection for an unknown positive regularity constant, conforming subdivision, and stopping rules. A source for the named method class is required.

children.title: DIRECT Selection-Bias Variants
children.top_down_role: Selection modifications addressing excessive global search, excessive local refinement, and candidate-set growth.

assumptions_latex: The objective is a deterministic function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) on a compact hyperrectangle \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\).
Each active rectangle has center value \(f(c_R)\) and a prescribed local size measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns the sampled incumbent after the stopping budget or tolerance is reached.

notation.meaning: locally biased size measure of rectangle R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally biased DIRECT template; the defining size measure must be checked against the selected DIRECT-L variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Normalize \(D\) to the unit cube, evaluate its center, and maintain a rectangular partition. At iteration \(k\), call a rectangle \(R\) potentially optimal when some \(L>0\) satisfies \(f(c_R)-L\delta_R^{L}\leq f(c_S)-L\delta_S^{L}\) for every active rectangle \(S\), together with the prescribed sufficient-improvement test relative to \(f_k^*\). Subdivide every selected rectangle along its longest coordinates, evaluate the new centers required by the partition, update \(f_k^*\), and terminate at the stated budget or tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DIRECT-L replaces the standard rectangle-size score with a locally biased measure, favoring finer rectangles while retaining potentially-optimal selection.
knowledge_statements.title: DIRECT-L Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role is appropriate, but DIRECT-L is defined by a specific locally biased size measure and associated selection rule. Neither the meaning of delta_R^L nor the sufficient-improvement test is specified or sourced.

assumptions_latex: The objective is a deterministic function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) on a compact hyperrectangle \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\).
A DIRECT phase has a finite stopping or stagnation rule, and a restart schedule is prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Return the best point sampled over all completed and current DIRECT phases.

notation.meaning: initial region or partition state for phase j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic restart wrapper; restart triggers and retained state distinguish named family members.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run a DIRECT phase from \(\mathcal{P}_0^0=\{D\}\) until its stopping time \(\tau_0\). After phase \(j\), retain the global incumbent \(x_j^*\). If the total budget remains, construct \(\mathcal{P}_{j+1}^0\) according to the prescribed restart rule, which may reset selection history, rescale the search region, or exclude previously refined rectangles, and start another DIRECT phase. Objective values at retained sample points need not be recomputed. Stop when the total budget is exhausted or the global termination condition holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DIRECT-Restart runs bounded DIRECT phases, preserves the incumbent, reinitializes selected search state after stagnation or a phase limit, and continues within a total budget.
knowledge_statements.title: DIRECT-Restart Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is only a generic restart wrapper. Resetting history, rescaling the region, and excluding rectangles are materially different restart mechanisms, so a family-specific source is needed to establish which operations characterize DIRECT-Restart.

assumptions_latex: The objective is a deterministic function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) on a compact hyperrectangle \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\).
Each rectangle has a center value, a size level, and a prescribed robustness or improvement test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method returns the best sampled center after its finite stopping condition is met.

notation.meaning: integer refinement level of rectangle R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provisional multilevel template; the named method's level schedule and robustness test require a primary source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain the DIRECT partition grouped by refinement level \(\ell_R\). At iteration \(k\), form each eligible set \(E_{k,l}\) using the prescribed robust improvement test relative to \(f_k^*\), and choose rectangles from one or more levels according to the multilevel schedule. Subdivide the chosen rectangles by the DIRECT longest-side rule, evaluate newly created centers, and update the incumbent. The schedule must revisit every required global level while permitting intensified refinement near competitive centers. Terminate at the evaluation, depth, or accuracy limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multilevel Robust DIRECT groups rectangles by refinement level and applies a robustness test and level schedule before ordinary DIRECT subdivision.
knowledge_statements.title: Multilevel Robust DIRECT

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but the defining robust improvement test, eligible sets, and multilevel schedule are unspecified. Without a primary source, the statement cannot be identified reliably with Multilevel Robust DIRECT.

assumptions_latex: A finite active set of DIRECT rectangles is available.
Every rectangle \(R\) has a size \(d_R\) and center value \(f(c_R)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only the reduced nondominated set is subdivided, and the incumbent is updated from the resulting samples.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-candidate Pareto selection template; the reduction rule is method-specific.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), construct a prescribed candidate subset \(C_k\subseteq\mathcal{R}_k\). Define \(R\in C_k\) to dominate \(S\in C_k\) when \(d_R\geq d_S\) and \(f(c_R)\leq f(c_S)\), with at least one strict inequality. Let \(P_k\) be the rectangles in \(C_k\) not dominated by another member of \(C_k\), optionally filtered by the stated sufficient-improvement condition. Subdivide every rectangle in \(P_k\) by the DIRECT rule, evaluate new centers, update the incumbent, and repeat until termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced-Set Pareto DIRECT constructs a smaller candidate pool, keeps its nondominated size-value rectangles, and subdivides only those survivors.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Set Pareto DIRECT

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated dominance orientation is mathematically coherent for minimizing objective value while favoring larger rectangles, but the construction of C_k and the exact Pareto or sufficient-improvement filtering are method-defining and unsupported.

assumptions_latex: The objective is a deterministic function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) on a compact hyperrectangle.
Every active rectangle has center \(c_R\), size \(d_R\), and distance to the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rectangles selected by the global and local criteria are subdivided, and the best sampled point is returned at termination.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global-local selection template; exact DIRECT-GL Pareto criteria require confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), form a global set \(G_k\) from rectangles nondominated under the prescribed objective-size criterion using \((f(c_R),d_R)\). Form a local set \(L_k\) from rectangles nondominated under the prescribed criterion combining objective value and proximity \(\lVert c_R-x_k^*\rVert\) to the incumbent. Apply any stated sufficient-improvement filters, then subdivide every rectangle in \(G_k\cup L_k\) by the DIRECT partition rule. Evaluate new centers, update \(x_k^*\), and stop at the evaluation or accuracy limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DIRECT-GL combines globally exploratory size-value selection with a second criterion favoring rectangles near the incumbent, then subdivides their union.
knowledge_statements.title: DIRECT-GL Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role matches the family container, but the global and local nondominance criteria are only placeholders. A primary DIRECT-GL source is needed to verify the objectives, distance term, filters, and union rule.

children.title: DIRECT Hybrid Acceleration
children.top_down_role: In-scope acceleration families that retain DIRECT as the global partition engine.

assumptions_latex: The objective is a deterministic function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) on a compact hyperrectangle.
The local solver accepts a sampled start and returns a feasible point with no larger objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hybrid returns the best point produced by either DIRECT sampling or an invoked local-search run.

notation.meaning: set of previously used local starts

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic deterministic hybrid with explicit triggering and incumbent reintegration.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.2 'Globalized' Local Optimization Strategies, Combined with Grid Search or Random Search p. 24

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run DIRECT while maintaining incumbent \(x_k^*\). When the prescribed trigger holds and \(x_k^*\notin H_k\), invoke the local solver and set \(y_k=\mathcal{L}(x_k^*)\). Add \(x_k^*\) to \(H_k\), evaluate or validate \(f(y_k)\), and replace the incumbent when \(f(y_k)<f(x_k^*)\). Continue the DIRECT partition process, optionally inserting \(y_k\) into its sample history according to the stated reintegration rule. Stop when the combined evaluation budget or convergence condition is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hybrid periodically launches local search from a DIRECT incumbent, accepts improvement, prevents redundant launches, and continues global partition search.
knowledge_statements.title: DIRECT–Local Search Hybrids

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.2 'Globalized' Local Optimization Strategies, Combined with Grid Search or Random Search p. 24

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited section concerns globalized local optimization combined with grid or random search and does not specifically support this DIRECT hybrid template. The trigger, duplicate-start test, acceptance condition, and reintegration rule require DIRECT-specific evidence.

assumptions_latex: The objective is a deterministic function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) on a compact hyperrectangle.
The accelerator produces trial points inside a selected DIRECT rectangle and uses a finite evaluation allowance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The incumbent includes accelerator evaluations, while the enclosing DIRECT partition remains available for subsequent global iterations.

notation.meaning: finite accelerator trial set in R_k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic accelerator embedded within DIRECT without replacing the global partition mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After a prescribed DIRECT selection step, choose a promising rectangle \(R_k\) and generate a finite trial set \(A_k\subseteq R_k\) by the designated local accelerator. Evaluate \(f\) on previously unevaluated members of \(A_k\), update \(x_k^*\), and record all evaluations. The accelerator neither discards unselected DIRECT rectangles nor consumes more than its assigned allowance. Resume potentially-optimal rectangle selection using the updated sample history and terminate when the shared evaluation budget or accuracy condition is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DIRECT local accelerator spends a bounded set of extra evaluations inside a promising rectangle, updates the incumbent, and then resumes global partition search.
knowledge_statements.title: DIRECT Local Accelerators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record describes a plausible generic accelerator wrapper, but it does not identify or source the accelerator, its trigger, trial-set construction, or how off-center evaluations affect subsequent DIRECT selection.

assumptions_latex: The objective is expensive and deterministic on a compact hyperrectangle \(D\).
A surrogate fitting rule and an exact-evaluation safeguard are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the best exactly evaluated point, never merely the minimizer predicted by the metamodel.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Surrogate-assisted DIRECT template retaining exact-evaluation safeguards.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.2 Methods Based on Statistical Models p. 17

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize DIRECT with an archive \(\mathcal{D}_0\) of exact evaluations. At iteration \(k\), fit \(\widehat f_k\) to \(\mathcal{D}_k\), use its predictions or uncertainty measure to rank or screen candidate rectangles, and form \(E_k\). Evaluate the true objective at the prescribed new points of rectangles in \(E_k\), append the results to \(\mathcal{D}_{k+1}\), and update the incumbent. A safeguard must force exact evaluation of rectangles required by the underlying global exploration schedule. Stop at the exact-evaluation budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metamodel-assisted DIRECT screens or ranks rectangles with a surrogate but periodically enforces true evaluations and returns the best exactly evaluated point.
knowledge_statements.title: Metamodel-Assisted DIRECT

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.2 Methods Based on Statistical Models p. 17

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited general section on statistical models does not substantiate a metamodel-assisted DIRECT algorithm. The surrogate, acquisition or screening rule, exact-evaluation set, and claimed global-exploration safeguard require method-specific evidence.

children.title: Constrained DIRECT Methods
children.top_down_role: DIRECT-type methods for explicit, hidden, and simulation-defined feasibility.

assumptions_latex: The constrained problem is \(\min\{f(x):x\in D,\ g_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) with compact hyperrectangle \(D\).
Objective and constraint values are available at every sampled point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned incumbent is the sampled point with smallest penalized value, with feasibility reported separately.

notation.meaning: positive penalty parameter at iteration k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exterior-penalty DIRECT template with an iteration-dependent penalty parameter.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Penalty Methods p. 59

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\rho_0>0\), evaluate the initial DIRECT sample, and assign every sampled point the value \(F_k(x)=f(x)+\rho_kV(x)\). At iteration \(k\), apply the DIRECT potentially-optimal rectangle rule with center values \(F_k(c_R)\), subdivide selected rectangles, and evaluate \(f\) and every \(g_i\) at new centers. Update \(\rho_k\) by the prescribed nondecreasing penalty schedule and recompute stored penalized values when it changes. Terminate at the budget or feasibility-accuracy condition, reporting both the penalized incumbent and its violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Penalty-based DIRECT applies ordinary rectangle selection to objective plus weighted constraint violation, updates the penalty, and reports the incumbent's feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Penalty-Based DIRECT

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Penalty Methods p. 59

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited general penalty-method section does not support this specific integration with DIRECT or the nondecreasing penalty schedule. Moreover, returning the smallest penalized value need not yield the preferred feasible incumbent, so variant-specific sourcing is required for the update and reporting semantics.

assumptions_latex: The search domain is a compact box \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), partitioned into axis-aligned rectangles sampled at their centers.
The objective \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) and constraint functions \(g_j:D\to\mathbb{R}\), \(j=1,\ldots,m\), are evaluable at every sampled center.
A point is feasible exactly when \(g_j(x)\le 0\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method returns the feasible sampled center having the smallest observed objective value, or reports that no feasible sampled center was found.

notation.meaning: center and size measure of rectangle R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic lexicographic feasibility-first constrained DIRECT; published variants may use different secondary rankings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with the rectangle \(D\) and evaluate its center. At each iteration, assign every current rectangle \(R\) the feasibility-priority key \[K_R=\begin{cases}(0,f(c_R),-d_R),&v(c_R)=0,\\(1,v(c_R),-d_R),&v(c_R)>0.\end{cases}\] Select one or more rectangles minimal under \(\preceq_{\mathrm{lex}}\), subdivide each selected rectangle by the prescribed DIRECT longest-side trisection, and evaluate all newly created centers. Thus any sampled feasible rectangle ranks ahead of every sampled infeasible rectangle; objective value ranks feasible rectangles, while violation ranks infeasible rectangles. Stop at a stated evaluation or iteration budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank feasible rectangles before infeasible ones, then rank them by objective or violation respectively, refine selected rectangles, and return the best feasible sampled center.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Priority DIRECT

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf, but the lexicographic key is a specific constrained-DIRECT variant rather than a uniquely standard feasibility-priority rule. No inspectable citation supports the ranking, tie handling, subdivision behavior, or output convention.

assumptions_latex: The domain \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a compact box with a finite axis-aligned rectangular partition at every iteration.
Every sampled center admits objective and constraint evaluations.
The selection rule compares rectangles through both constraint violation and rectangle size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, the reported point minimizes \(v\) among sampled centers if none is feasible; otherwise it minimizes \(f\) among sampled feasible centers.

notation.meaning: center and size measure of rectangle R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Violation-driven constrained DIRECT with feasibility retained as the ultimate output criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\mathcal P_0=\{D\}\) and evaluate its center. At iteration \(k\), form the lower tradeoff envelope of the points \(\{(d_R,v(c_R)):R\in\mathcal P_k\}\): select each \(R\) for which some \(L>0\) satisfies \[v(c_R)-Ld_R\le v(c_Q)-Ld_Q\quad\text{for every }Q\in\mathcal P_k.\] If feasible sampled centers exist, also retain a rectangle containing a currently best feasible center among the candidates. Subdivide selected rectangles by DIRECT trisection, evaluate new centers, and repeat until the prescribed budget is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select rectangles that optimally trade center violation against size, preserve a best feasible candidate when available, and repeatedly apply DIRECT subdivision.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Violation Selection DIRECT

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf, but the proposed violation-size lower-envelope rule and retention of a best-feasible rectangle are variant-specific and uncited. A source is required to determine the correct selection formula and hypotheses.

assumptions_latex: The nominal domain \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a compact box.
An evaluation either returns a finite value \(f(x)\) or declares \(x\) undefined, without an explicit algebraic constraint description.
DIRECT subdivisions and center evaluations are otherwise well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the sampled defined point with minimum objective value; undefined centers are excluded from incumbent comparison and their rectangles remain represented by the stated surrogate.

notation.meaning: set of sampled points with defined evaluations
finite surrogate assigned to an undefined center
center and size of rectangle R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite-surrogate hidden-constraint variant; rejection and neighborhood-surrogate variants require separate sourcing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Evaluate the initial center. At iteration \(k\), assign every rectangle \(R\) the merit \[\phi_k(R)=\begin{cases}f(c_R),&c_R\in S_k^{\mathrm{def}},\\M_k,&c_R\notin S_k^{\mathrm{def}},\end{cases}\] where \(M_k\) is a stated finite value no smaller than the largest defined value observed by iteration \(k\). Apply the ordinary DIRECT size-merit selection rule to \((d_R,\phi_k(R))\), subdivide selected rectangles, and evaluate their new centers. Continue through undefined rectangles only when their size makes them selectable. Stop at the evaluation budget and return \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S_k^{\mathrm{def}}}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent failed evaluations by a finite adverse surrogate, retain size-driven exploration of their rectangles, and return the best point where the objective was defined.
knowledge_statements.title: Hidden-Constraint DIRECT

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf, but assigning every failed evaluation a finite surrogate no smaller than the largest defined value is only one possible hidden-constraint policy. No source supports this policy or guarantees that undefined rectangles remain selectable as stated.

children.title: DIRECT Dense-Partition Convergence
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic convergence families based on exhaustive scale refinement, dense representative sampling, and accumulation near global optimizers.

assumptions_latex: The compact box \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is covered by a nested sequence of finite rectangular partitions \((\mathcal P_k)_{k\ge0}\).
Every refinement replaces a selected rectangle by finitely many rectangles whose maximum diameter is at most a fixed factor \(\rho<1\) times its diameter.
Every rectangle created by the process is selected for refinement after finitely many subsequent iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mesh size converges to zero: \(\lim_{k\to\infty}\max_{R\in\mathcal P_k}\operatorname{diam}(R)=0\).

notation.meaning: largest rectangle diameter at iteration k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract exhaustive-refinement result underlying dense-partition convergence, independent of a particular DIRECT tie rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated assumptions, exhaustive refinement prevents any positive rectangle diameter from persisting indefinitely. Consequently, \[h_k=\max_{R\in\mathcal P_k}\operatorname{diam}(R)\longrightarrow0.\] Equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(K\) such that every rectangle in \(\mathcal P_k\) has diameter below \(\varepsilon\) whenever \(k\ge K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every created rectangle is eventually refined and refinement uniformly contracts diameter, then the largest rectangle diameter tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Exhaustive-Refinement Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is mathematically plausible and its kind fits the convergence leaf, but it has no citation. An inspectable source is needed for the exhaustive-refinement hypothesis and its relationship to DIRECT dense-partition convergence.

assumptions_latex: The hypotheses of exhaustive-refinement convergence hold on the compact box \(D\).
Each rectangle is sampled at a representative point lying in that rectangle, in particular at its center.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The complete sample sequence is dense in \(D\): for every \(x\in D\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), some sampled center \(c_k\) satisfies \(\lVert c_k-x\rVert_2<\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: sequence of all sampled rectangle centers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density follows from vanishing partition mesh and representative points contained in their rectangles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((c_k)_{k\ge1}\) list every sampled center. Since the partition mesh tends to zero, every point of \(D\) lies in rectangles of arbitrarily small diameter whose representative centers are sampled. Hence \[\overline{\{c_k:k\ge1\}}=D.\] In quantified form, for each \(x\in D\) and each \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an index \(k\) such that \(\lVert c_k-x\rVert_2<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing partition diameter makes the collection of sampled rectangle centers dense throughout the compact search box.
knowledge_statements.title: Center-Sample Density

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits the leaf, and density follows under an appropriate vanishing-mesh and sampling convention. No citation establishes that convention for the intended DIRECT process, so the exact hypotheses remain unsupported.

assumptions_latex: The search box \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact and the sampled centers \((c_k)\) are dense in \(D\).
The objective \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous.
At stage \(k\), the incumbent \(x_k\) is a minimum-value point among \(c_1,\ldots,c_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accumulation point of \((x_k)\) belongs to \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x)\), and \(f(x_k)\to f^*=\min_{x\in D}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-objective consequence of dense deterministic sampling on a compact box.

source_refs.locator: 8.4 Proof of Convergence to the Global Minimum p. 282

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((c_k)_{k\ge1}\) be dense in the compact box \(D\), let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous, and choose \(x_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\le i\le k}f(c_i)\). Then \[f(x_k)\longrightarrow f^*=\min_{x\in D}f(x).\] Every accumulation point \(\bar x\) of \((x_k)\) belongs to \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x)\). If \(X^*=\{x^*\}\), then \(x_k\to x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous objective on a compact box, dense sampling makes incumbent values converge to the global minimum; every incumbent accumulation point is globally minimizing, and a unique global minimizer attracts the full incumbent sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Global-Minimizer Accumulation

source_witnesses.locator: 8.4 Proof of Convergence to the Global Minimum p. 282

assumptions_latex: The objective \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous on a compact box \(D\), and the sampled centers are dense.
Only point evaluations and the partition history are used; no certified global lower bound is maintained.
The algorithm may stop after any finite number of evaluations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f(x_k)\to f^*\), finite data alone do not generally certify that \(f(x_k)-f^*\le\varepsilon\) for a prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\).

notation.meaning: best sampled point after k evaluations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes asymptotic dense-sampling convergence from finite epsilon-global certification.

source_refs.locator: 3.6 Finite epsilon-Convergence and epsilon-Global Optimality p. 87

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated assumptions, the incumbent values satisfy \[f(x_k)\longrightarrow f^*=\min_{x\in D}f(x).\] Nevertheless, for a prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\), observations from an arbitrary finite run do not generally imply \[f(x_k)-f^*\le\varepsilon.\] A finite global-optimality certificate requires additional valid information, such as a regularity modulus, a certified global lower bound, or a finite exhaustive enclosure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense sampling gives asymptotic convergence to the global value, but a finite run does not generally certify a prescribed global-optimality gap without additional valid bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Convergence Without Finite Certification

source_witnesses.locator: 3.6 Finite epsilon-Convergence and epsilon-Global Optimality p. 87

children.title: DIRECT Failure-Slowdown Regimes
children.top_down_role: Principal exploration, refinement, representative-sampling, and dimension-scaling weaknesses identified in the DIRECT literature.

assumptions_latex: At each iteration, the selection rule refines at least one rectangle of maximal current diameter.
A local-refinement phase also repeatedly selects a rectangle containing the incumbent.
Every selected rectangle requires at least one new objective evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After \(T\) local-refinement iterations, at least \(T\) evaluations are spent on globally coarse rectangles, so the global-exploration overhead is \(\Omega(T)\).

notation.meaning: number of evaluations outside the incumbent rectangle chain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional evaluation-overhead bound for compulsory global refinement during an extended local phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a local phase lasts \(T\) iterations and, at every one of those iterations, the selection rule also chooses a rectangle of diameter \(d_k^{\max}\) outside the incumbent refinement chain. If refining that coarse rectangle costs at least one new evaluation, then \[N_{\mathrm{global}}(T)\ge T.\] Hence compulsory preservation of a globally coarse candidate imposes linear evaluation overhead during local refinement, even when the incumbent neighborhood is already correctly identified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If each local-refinement iteration must also split a globally coarse rectangle, at least one globally directed evaluation is incurred per iteration.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Drag During Local Refinement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role is appropriate, but the assumptions only require refinement of a maximal-diameter rectangle, whereas the conclusion counts an evaluation outside the incumbent refinement chain. That outside-chain condition appears only in the statement and is not guaranteed by the listed assumptions. The DIRECT selection and cost model are also uncited.

assumptions_latex: DIRECT ranks rectangles through sampled center values and rectangle sizes.
A suboptimal basin contains sampled centers whose values are temporarily lower than those sampled outside it.
No certified lower bound eliminates that basin before its rectangles become sufficiently small.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm can perform arbitrarily many refinements inside a basin containing no global minimizer before another basin becomes preferable under the selection rule.

notation.meaning: minimum objective over the suboptimal basin

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mechanism-level failure boundary; the delay depends on selection and tie-handling details.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\subset D\) satisfy \(f_B^*>f^*\), but suppose its currently sampled centers have lower values than every sampled center in \(D\setminus B\). A size-value selection rule may then keep rectangles in \(B\) on its potentially optimal envelope while their diameters contract. For every prescribed \(M\), objective geometry and initial samples can make this ordering persist for the first \(M\) selections. Thus asymptotic global convergence does not preclude arbitrarily long overrefinement of a basin that contains no global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Misleading center values can keep a suboptimal basin selectable for arbitrarily many refinements, despite eventual global convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Suboptimal-Basin Overrefinement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but the assumptions do not establish the quantified claim that overrefinement can persist for every prescribed number of selections. A sourced DIRECT construction or theorem is required to support that conclusion and its dependence on selection and tie policies.

assumptions_latex: The sample sequence \((c_k)\) in a compact box \(D\) is not dense.
The algorithm bases its incumbent only on sampled objective values.
Objectives are allowed to be continuous on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a continuous objective whose unique global minimizer lies in an unsampled open region, so the incumbent values fail to converge to the global minimum.

notation.meaning: an open ball disjoint from the sample closure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic continuous counterexample showing why dense exploration is necessary for universal convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because the samples are not dense, choose a nonempty open ball \(B\subset D\) whose closure is disjoint from \(S\). Let \(\psi:D\to[0,1]\) be continuous, supported in \(B\), and attain its unique maximum \(1\) at \(x^*\in B\). Define \(f=-\psi\). Every sampled point satisfies \(f(c_k)=0\), while \(f(x^*)=-1\). Consequently every sampled incumbent has value \(0\) and never approaches the global minimum \(-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any nondense sampling policy can miss an open region containing a continuous objective's unique global minimizer forever.
knowledge_statements.title: Insufficient Global Exploration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is a standard consequence of nondense deterministic sampling, and its kind fits the failure leaf. However, no citation supports the construction or connects the generic nondensity premise to the intended DIRECT exploration regime.

assumptions_latex: A deterministic partition method observes an objective only at one representative point of each sampled rectangle.
The resulting representative-point set \(S\) omits a nonempty open ball \(B\subset D\).
The admissible objective class contains continuous functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Representative-point data cannot distinguish the constant objective from a continuous objective having a strict minimum inside \(B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic ambiguity caused by sampling only rectangle representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_0(x)=0\) on \(D\). Choose a continuous bump \(\psi:D\to[0,1]\) supported in \(B\), with \(\psi(x^*)=1\) at a unique point \(x^*\in B\), and define \(f_1=-\psi\). Then \[f_0(s)=f_1(s)=0\quad\text{for every }s\in S,\] but \(\min_D f_0=0\) whereas \(\min_D f_1=-1\). Thus representative-point observations alone are uninformative about objective behavior hidden between those points unless refinement makes the representatives dense or additional regularity bounds are used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two continuous objectives can agree at every representative sample while one hides a strict minimum between samples.
knowledge_statements.title: Uninformative Representative-Point Sampling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample role is suitable and the indistinguishability claim is mathematically plausible, but it is uncited. A source should support the representative-point information limitation and clarify its distinction from the sibling nondense-exploration counterexample.

assumptions_latex: At some iteration, \(m\) congruent maximal-diameter rectangles have identical center values.
The implementation selects every rectangle tied on the relevant size-value envelope.
Splitting one such rectangle along \(q\ge1\) longest coordinates requires at least \(2q\) new center evaluations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: That iteration requires at least \(2qm\) new evaluations; hence unresolved ties can make a single iteration's evaluation cost grow linearly with the tie multiplicity.

notation.meaning: number of longest coordinates split per rectangle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional per-iteration cost bound for all-ties selection under standard coordinate trisection sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(m\) rectangles share the same maximal diameter and center value, their size-value representations coincide. Under an all-ties rule, all \(m\) are selected. If splitting each rectangle along \(q\) longest coordinates evaluates two displaced centers per coordinate, then \[N_{\mathrm{new}}\ge 2qm.\] Therefore large equal-value plateaus or symmetric partitions can proliferate selected ties and produce expensive iterations even though the rectangles carry duplicate selection information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selecting all identical size-value ties costs at least two new evaluations per split coordinate and tied rectangle.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Tie Proliferation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the leaf and the arithmetic follows from the stated conditional cost model. However, selecting all tied rectangles and requiring two new evaluations per longest coordinate are implementation-specific DIRECT conventions with no supporting citation.

knowledge_statements.title: DIRECT Dimensionality Barrier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential box growth under isotropic ternary refinement in a DIRECT-style search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the initial domain be the unit box in dimension \(d\). A full ternary refinement of every coordinate produces \(3^d\) congruent subboxes; after \(m\) such levels there are \(3^{md}\) subboxes, each with Euclidean radius \(r_m=\sqrt d/(2\,3^m)\). Consequently, any regime that must inspect every box to guarantee resolution \(r_m\leq\delta\) requires at least \[3^{md}\geq\left(\frac{\sqrt d}{2\delta}\right)^d\] representative evaluations up to constant reuse factors. Thus DIRECT's partition mechanism does not remove exponential dimensional dependence when no boxes can be safely excluded by objective information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If DIRECT must refine essentially all ternary boxes, attaining geometric resolution δ requires on the order of δ^{-d} boxes, exposing an exponential dimensional barrier.
assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb N\) and the domain is \([0,1]^d\).
Refinement trisects every coordinate uniformly.
No objective-based pruning excludes a positive fraction of boxes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\delta)\geq (\sqrt d/(2\delta))^d\) in the exhaustive-refinement regime.

notation.meaning: number of full ternary refinement levels
Euclidean radius of a level-m subbox

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dimensional-growth calculation is plausible for exhaustive isotropic grid refinement, but no source supports its attribution to DIRECT. Standard DIRECT does not simply refine every coordinate of every box at every level. Moreover, failure to exclude a positive fraction of boxes does not imply that every box is inspected, as required by the displayed lower bound.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Accuracy Refinement Slowdown
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case accuracy cost when Lipschitz bounds cannot prune ternary partition cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz in Euclidean distance and a ternary partition search samples one representative per surviving level-\(m\) box. A box radius at most \(\varepsilon/L\) is sufficient for representative-point error at most \(\varepsilon\). Under uniform refinement this requires \(m\geq\lceil\log_3(L\sqrt d/(2\varepsilon))\rceil\). If bounds fail to eliminate boxes, the surviving population satisfies \[N_\varepsilon=3^{md}\geq\left(\frac{L\sqrt d}{2\varepsilon}\right)^d.\] Hence the worst-case work grows polynomially in \(1/\varepsilon\) with exponent \(d\), causing severe slowdown at high accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without effective pruning, reducing Lipschitz error to ε requires roughly (L/ε)^d ternary cells, so high-accuracy refinement rapidly becomes expensive.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \([0,1]^d\).
Each surviving box is represented by an evaluated point.
All level-\(m\) boxes survive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\varepsilon\geq (L\sqrt d/(2\varepsilon))^d\).

notation.meaning: surviving representative evaluations needed at that accuracy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exhaustive ternary-grid accuracy calculation is mathematically plausible, but no citation supports its use as a DIRECT-specific slowdown statement or the representative-evaluation counting convention. An inspectable DIRECT or partition-search complexity source is required.

children.title: Bound-Based Optimality Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificate families derived from valid global envelopes, regional bounds, and incumbent comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Lower-Envelope Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz lower envelope and its induced global optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be compact, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz, and let observations be \(y_i=f(x_i)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). Define \[\ell_n(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\{y_i-Ld(x,x_i)\},\qquad B_n=\min_{x\in X}\ell_n(x),\qquad U_n=\min_i y_i.\] Every \(L\)-Lipschitz function consistent with the observations satisfies \(f(x)\geq\ell_n(x)\) on \(X\). Therefore \(B_n\leq f^*:=\min_X f\leq U_n\), and the computable gap \(U_n-B_n\) certifies the incumbent's global suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum of sample-centered Lipschitz cones is a valid global lower envelope; its minimum and the incumbent value give a certified optimality gap.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a compact metric space.
\(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz with known \(L\).
Observations are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_n\leq f^*\leq U_n\) and \(U_n-f^*\leq U_n-B_n\).

source_refs.locator: 1.1.4 Lipschitz Global Optimization p. 14

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.4 Lipschitz Global Optimization p. 14

knowledge_statements.title: Regional Bound Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction of a Lipschitz lower envelope to a partition region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under exact observations of an \(L\)-Lipschitz function on compact \((X,d)\), let \(\ell_n(x)=\max_i\{f(x_i)-Ld(x,x_i)\}\). For any nonempty compact region \(R\subseteq X\), define \[B_n(R)=\min_{x\in R}\ell_n(x).\] Since \(\ell_n(x)\leq f(x)\) throughout \(X\), the value \(B_n(R)\) satisfies \(B_n(R)\leq\min_{x\in R}f(x)\). Given an incumbent value \(U_n\), the inequality \(B_n(R)\geq U_n-\varepsilon\) certifies that no point in \(R\) can improve the incumbent by more than \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing the Lipschitz lower envelope over a region gives a valid regional bound and can certify that the region contains no significant improvement.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is compact and \(R\subseteq X\) is nonempty and compact.
\(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz with exact observations.
\(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_n(R)\leq\min_R f\), and \(B_n(R)\geq U_n-\varepsilon\) excludes improvements exceeding \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: certified lower bound over the region

source_refs.locator: 2.7 Partition Strategies in General Lipschitz Optimization p. 131

source_witnesses.locator: 2.7 Partition Strategies in General Lipschitz Optimization p. 131

knowledge_statements.title: Prescribed-Accuracy Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute-error certification from matching global upper and lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f^*=\min_{x\in X}f(x)\). Suppose an evaluated feasible point \(\hat x_n\) supplies \(U_n=f(\hat x_n)\), while a valid global relaxation supplies \(B_n\leq f^*\). For prescribed absolute accuracy \(\varepsilon\geq0\), the checkable inequality \[U_n-B_n\leq\varepsilon\] certifies \(0\leq f(\hat x_n)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\). A relative certificate may instead use \(U_n-B_n\leq\varepsilon\max\{1,|U_n|\}\), provided this scaling convention is declared before the search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incumbent is ε-globally optimal whenever its value differs from a valid global lower bound by at most ε.
assumptions_latex: \(B_n\leq f^*\leq U_n\).
\(U_n=f(\hat x_n)\) for a feasible evaluated point.
\(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_n-B_n\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow f(\hat x_n)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\).

source_refs.locator: 2.7 Partition Strategies in General Lipschitz Optimization p. 131

source_witnesses.locator: 2.7 Partition Strategies in General Lipschitz Optimization p. 131

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer-Enclosure Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certified enclosure obtained by excluding points whose lower envelope exceeds the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\ell_n:X\to\mathbb R\) be a certified pointwise lower bound for \(f\), and let \(U_n=f(\hat x_n)\) be an incumbent value. Define the retained set \[E_n=\{x\in X:\ell_n(x)\leq U_n\}.\] Every global minimizer \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\) belongs to \(E_n\), because \(\ell_n(x^*)\leq f(x^*)\leq U_n\). More generally, \(E_n(\varepsilon)=\{x:\ell_n(x)\leq U_n-\varepsilon\}\) contains every point capable of improving the incumbent by at least \(\varepsilon\); its complement is therefore safely excludable for that improvement target.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Points whose certified lower bound exceeds the incumbent cannot be global minimizers; the remaining sublevel set encloses every optimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is compact and a global minimizer exists.
\(\ell_n(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
\(U_n\) is the value of a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_X f\subseteq E_n\).

source_refs.locator: 2.7 Partition Strategies in General Lipschitz Optimization p. 131

source_witnesses.locator: 2.7 Partition Strategies in General Lipschitz Optimization p. 131

children.title: Termination Regimes
children.top_down_role: Rigorous and practical termination families, with certified rules ordered before resource-based rules.

knowledge_statements.title: Certified Bound-Gap Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination rule based on a globally valid lower bound and feasible incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(n\), let \(U_n\) be the value of an evaluated feasible incumbent and let \(B_n\) be a certified lower bound on \(f^*=\min_X f\). For an absolute tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), certified bound-gap termination occurs when \[U_n-B_n\leq\varepsilon.\] The algorithm returns the incumbent \(\hat x_n\), for which \(f(\hat x_n)=U_n\). The stopping condition implies \(0\leq f(\hat x_n)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\); unlike budget or stagnation stopping, it therefore carries a global accuracy guarantee under the validity of \(B_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop when the incumbent and a valid global lower bound differ by at most ε; the returned point is then globally ε-optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(B_n\leq f^*\leq U_n\).
\(U_n=f(\hat x_n)\) for a feasible incumbent.
\(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_n-B_n\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow f(\hat x_n)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\).

source_refs.locator: 2.7 Partition Strategies in General Lipschitz Optimization p. 131

source_witnesses.locator: 2.7 Partition Strategies in General Lipschitz Optimization p. 131

knowledge_statements.title: Regional Exhaustion Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination after every covering region is certified unable to improve the incumbent materially.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite family \(\mathcal R_n\) cover \(X\), and let each region \(R\in\mathcal R_n\) have a certified bound \(B_n(R)\leq\min_{x\in R}f(x)\). Given incumbent value \(U_n\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), declare \(R\) exhausted when \(B_n(R)\geq U_n-\varepsilon\). Regional exhaustion termination occurs when every covering region is exhausted. Then \(f^*=\min_X f\geq\min_R B_n(R)\geq U_n-\varepsilon\), so the incumbent is globally \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If certified bounds show that every covering region cannot improve the incumbent by more than ε, search may terminate with an ε-optimal solution.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\bigcup_{R\in\mathcal R_n}R\).
\(B_n(R)\leq\min_R f\) for every region.
\(U_n\) is a feasible incumbent value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall R,\ B_n(R)\geq U_n-\varepsilon\Rightarrow U_n-f^*\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: finite covering family of active or exhausted regions

source_refs.locator: 2.7 Partition Strategies in General Lipschitz Optimization p. 131

source_witnesses.locator: 2.7 Partition Strategies in General Lipschitz Optimization p. 131

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric-Resolution Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stopping after every partition cell has sufficiently small covering radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R_n\) cover compact \(X\). For every \(R\in\mathcal R_n\), suppose an evaluated representative \(c_R\in R\) is available and define \(r_R=\sup_{x\in R}d(x,c_R)\). If \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, geometric-resolution termination at tolerance \(\delta>0\) occurs when \[\max_{R\in\mathcal R_n}r_R\leq\delta.\] Returning the best representative \(\hat x_n\) then guarantees \(f(\hat x_n)-f^*\leq L\delta\). Thus choosing \(\delta\leq\varepsilon/L\) yields an absolute \(\varepsilon\)-optimality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every cell lies within δ of an evaluated representative, the best representative is globally accurate within Lδ for an L-Lipschitz objective.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is compact and covered by \(\mathcal R_n\).
\(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz.
Each region has an evaluated representative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_R r_R\leq\delta\Rightarrow f(\hat x_n)-f^*\leq L\delta\).

notation.meaning: covering radius of region R about its representative

source_refs.locator: 2.7 Partition Strategies in General Lipschitz Optimization p. 131

source_witnesses.locator: 2.7 Partition Strategies in General Lipschitz Optimization p. 131

knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation-Budget Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource-limited stopping rule without an intrinsic optimality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an evaluation budget \(N_{\max}\in\mathbb N\). Let \(N_n\) denote the number of objective evaluations completed by iteration \(n\). Evaluation-budget termination occurs before requesting any evaluation that would make \(N_n>N_{\max}\); the algorithm returns the best feasible point evaluated so far. This condition guarantees only the resource bound \(N_n\leq N_{\max}\). Unless an independent lower bound, covering condition, or probabilistic guarantee is also satisfied, it implies no prescribed bound on the returned point's global suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop before exceeding a fixed evaluation budget and return the best sampled point; the budget alone gives no global accuracy certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(N_{\max}\in\mathbb N\) is fixed before termination.
Objective evaluations are counted consistently.
At least one feasible point has been evaluated.

knowledge_statements.title: Stagnation-Based Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Heuristic stopping after insufficient incumbent improvement over a fixed window.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U_n\) be the nonincreasing incumbent sequence of a minimization method. Fix a window \(w\in\mathbb N\) and threshold \(\eta\geq0\). Stagnation-based termination occurs at iteration \(n\geq w\) when \[U_{n-w}-U_n\leq\eta.\] The algorithm returns the current incumbent. This predicate measures recent observed improvement only: without an accompanying global lower bound or exhaustive geometric condition, it does not imply that the incumbent is globally or locally optimal, nor that future refinement cannot yield an improvement exceeding \(\eta\).

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Based Lipschitz Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic worst-case lower bound for sampled-point optimization of Lipschitz functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider deterministic adaptive algorithms that evaluate an unknown \(L\)-Lipschitz function on \([0,1]^d\), with distance \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\), and return one of \(n\) evaluated points. For the class of all such functions, worst-case simple regret satisfies \[\inf_A\sup_f\left(f(A(f))-\min_{x\in[0,1]^d}f(x)\right)\geq\frac{L}{2n^{1/d}}.\] Consequently, guaranteeing regret at most \(\varepsilon>0\) requires \(n\geq(L/(2\varepsilon))^d\) evaluations in this information model. Adaptive placement cannot remove this exponential dependence without additional structure beyond Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For arbitrary d-dimensional Lipschitz functions, deterministic sampled-point optimization needs at least order (L/ε)^d evaluations to guarantee ε simple regret.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Hull Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone-chain construction for lower-envelope candidates represented by size-value points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finitely many pairs \((d_i,v_i)\in\mathbb R^2\), first retain, for each repeated abscissa \(d_i\), only a pair having minimum ordinate. Sort the retained points by increasing abscissa. Initialize an empty stack \(H\); for each sorted point \(p\), repeatedly delete the last point of \(H\) while \(|H|\ge 2\) and the oriented cross product of the last two points of \(H\) with \(p\) is nonpositive, then append \(p\). The output \(H=(h_1,\ldots,h_m)\) lists the lower convex-hull vertices from left to right, with strictly increasing consecutive slopes. Collinear interior points are omitted by this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort size-value points, remove dominated duplicates, and use a monotone stack to retain exactly the lower convex-hull vertices.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Hull Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Insertion update for an ordered lower hull after adding one size-value point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subset\mathbb R^2\) be finite, let \(H=(h_1,\ldots,h_m)\) be the lower-hull vertices of \(Q\) in strictly increasing abscissa order, and let \(p=(d,v)\in\mathbb R^2\). If \(H\) contains \((d,v_0)\) with \(v_0\le v\), return \(H\). Otherwise remove the vertex with abscissa \(d\), if present, and insert \(p\) in abscissa order. Maintain a queue of triples consecutive in the current sequence that meet the insertion position or a position exposed by a deletion. Whenever a queued triple \((a,b,c)\) satisfies \(\operatorname{cross}(b-a,c-a)\le0\), delete its middle point \(b\) and enqueue the newly adjacent triples. Stop when the queue is empty. The resulting sequence is the lower convex-hull vertex sequence of \(Q\cup\{p\}\), with collinear interior points omitted; vertices outside the contiguous chain reached by these deletions remain unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insert the new point by abscissa, then repeatedly delete the middle point of each locally affected non-left-turn triple until all consecutive lower-hull slopes increase strictly.

knowledge_statements.title: Hull Degeneracy Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic conventions for coincident, collinear, and numerically ambiguous hull points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix tolerances \(\tau_d,\tau_v,\tau_o\ge0\). Treat points \((d_i,v_i)\) and \((d_j,v_j)\) as sharing an abscissa when \(|d_i-d_j|\le\tau_d\), retaining the smaller ordinate and a deterministic index on ties. Treat an orientation determinant as zero when its magnitude is at most \(\tau_o\); among a collinear lower-face chain retain its two extreme abscissae. Declare ordinates tied when their difference is at most \(\tau_v\). All dominance, orientation, and tie decisions must use these same conventions. With zero tolerances this produces a canonical exact lower hull; with positive tolerances it produces a deterministic tolerance-dependent approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolve duplicate abscissae, collinearity, and near ties by fixed tolerances and deterministic representatives.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau_d,\tau_v,\tau_o\ge0\) are fixed throughout a hull update.
Each point has a stable deterministic index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every degenerate input receives a reproducible lower-hull representation under the stated conventions.
